91.event_title: Vaclav Havel's first New Year's address as president
91.event: Days after becoming president at the end of the Velvet Revolution, the playwright and former dissident Vaclav Havel gave a New Year's address that broke with the upbeat official messages of his communist predecessors. He told citizens plainly that their country was not flourishing and that the worst problem was a contaminated moral environment, in which people had grown used to saying something different from what they thought. He added that all had helped to sustain the old system, and lamented that values such as love, compassion and forgiveness had lost their depth in everyday life.
91.explanation: Havel's speech was valued precisely because it was honest and free of the comforting deceptions citizens had heard for forty years, yet it was spoken with warmth and shared responsibility rather than blame.
91.tie_back: The kural defines truly sweet words as those of people who have seen what is right, steeped in affection and free of deceit, and Havel's address joined truthfulness to goodwill in exactly that way.
91._accuracy_note: A good example of guileless, well-meant speech from one who had seen the truth, though its content was sobering rather than sweet in the ordinary sense.

92.event_title: Princess Diana shakes hands with an AIDS patient
92.event: In April 1987 Diana, Princess of Wales, opened the first hospital ward in the United Kingdom dedicated to patients with HIV and AIDS, at London's Middlesex Hospital. At a time when many people wrongly believed the virus could be spread by touch, she shook hands with a patient without wearing gloves. The photographed gesture was widely credited with helping to change public attitudes towards people with the disease.
92.explanation: A warm, open manner did more to help people with AIDS than any material gift could have, because it challenged fear and stigma directly.
92.tie_back: The kural ranks a glad face and a kind manner above even generous giving, and a single ungloved handshake changed more than donations alone could have.
92._accuracy_note: A strong case of warmth of manner outweighing material help, though the gesture was a touch rather than kind words.

93.event: On the evening of the opening day of the Second Vatican Council, Pope John XXIII came unexpectedly to his window to greet a large crowd holding candles in St Peter's Square. Speaking without a prepared text, he remarked that even the moon seemed to have hurried out to watch, called himself a brother speaking to them, and asked them to go home and give their children a caress from the Pope, to dry any tears and to say a good word. The improvised greeting became one of the best-remembered moments of his papacy.
93.explanation: The speech is remembered not for doctrine but for its warmth, simplicity and evident sincerity, which reached people far beyond the square.
93.tie_back: The kural says a welcoming face, a kindly gaze and sweet words that come from within are themselves virtue, and John XXIII's unscripted greeting was exactly such heartfelt kindness.
93._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's picture of warm, heartfelt words as virtue in itself, documented by the Vatican's own transcript.

94.event_title: Fred Rogers testifies to the US Senate for public television
94.event: When President Nixon proposed cutting the planned 20 million dollar budget of the new Corporation for Public Broadcasting by half, the children's television host Fred Rogers testified before the Senate Communications Subcommittee. In a calm, gentle statement he described how his programme dealt with the inner drama of childhood and recited the words of one of his songs. The subcommittee chairman, Senator John Pastore, said the testimony had given him goosebumps and that Rogers appeared to have earned the 20 million dollars.
94.explanation: Rogers won over a sceptical senator through gentle, sincere speech rather than argument or pressure, helping to protect the funding his work depended on.
94.tie_back: The kural promises that those who speak words that gladden everyone will not be overtaken by want, and Rogers's kindly words helped secure the support public broadcasting needed.
94._accuracy_note: A strong case of kind speech averting material want, though the final appropriation was decided by a wider political process.

95.event_title: Gandhi attends the royal reception at Buckingham Palace in his dhoti
95.event: While in London for the Second Round Table Conference on India's future, Mahatma Gandhi attended King George V's reception for the conference delegates at Buckingham Palace. He went in his customary dhoti, the garment the press called a loincloth, and slippers rather than formal court dress. Queen Mary recorded that he caused great excitement in what she called his odd get-up.
95.explanation: Gandhi treated humility and simplicity, not costly dress, as the proper adornment even at the most formal court in the world.
95.tie_back: The kural says humility and kind speech are a person's only real ornament, and Gandhi appeared before a king wearing nothing grander than his everyday dhoti.
95._accuracy_note: A vivid documented example of humility worn as one's ornament, though it illustrates the humility half of the kural more than kind speech.

96.event_title: Nelson Mandela appeals for calm after the killing of Chris Hani
96.event: On 10 April 1993 the South African Communist Party leader Chris Hani was assassinated, and the country, then in the middle of negotiations to end apartheid, faced the risk of widespread violence. Nelson Mandela, president of the African National Congress, went on national television that night and again on 13 April, appealing for discipline and calm, asking people to honour Hani through peaceful memorial services and urging that a date be fixed for democratic elections. Negotiations continued, and within weeks the date of the first democratic election, 27 April 1994, was agreed.
96.explanation: Carefully chosen, steadying words from a trusted leader helped hold a country back from violence at one of its most dangerous moments.
96.tie_back: The kural says that when a person seeks out what is good to say and says it well, evil wears away and virtue grows, and Mandela's addresses turned a moment of fury toward peaceful action.
96._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of deliberately chosen good words reducing harm, though the outcome also depended on many other actors.

97.event_title: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII on restraint in speech
97.event: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka had a series of edicts carved on rocks across his empire setting out his idea of dhamma. Rock Edict XII teaches that the root of growth in essentials for all religious groups is restraint in speech: people should not praise their own sect or condemn others without cause, and any criticism should be mild. It states that honouring other sects benefits both one's own and theirs, while disparaging them harms both.
97.explanation: Ashoka made gracious, restrained speech a matter of public policy, arguing that it served the speaker's own community as well as others.
97.tie_back: The kural says useful words that never depart from good character bring the speaker both goodwill and merit, and Ashoka's edict taught that courteous speech towards others enriches both speaker and hearer.
97._accuracy_note: A close parallel to the kural's claim that character-bound speech yields mutual benefit, though it is a documented teaching rather than an event showing the result.

98.event: As the Civil War neared its end, Abraham Lincoln took the oath of office for a second time and delivered a short address at the Capitol. He named slavery as the cause of the war but avoided triumph over the defeated South, closing with the words with malice toward none, with charity for all, and calling on the nation to bind up its wounds. The address is inscribed on the wall of the Lincoln Memorial.
98.explanation: At the moment of victory Lincoln chose words free of pettiness or revenge, and the speech remains one of the most admired in American history.
98.tie_back: The kural praises kind words with no trace of meanness, and Lincoln's address spoke to a defeated enemy without spite at the very moment he could have gloated.
98._accuracy_note: A strong example of speech purged of meanness, though the kural's promise of joy in this life and the next cannot be shown by any event.

99.event_title: The Seventeen-Article Constitution warns against anger
99.event: The Seventeen-Article Constitution, traditionally attributed to Prince Shotoku and dated to 604, set out moral principles for officials of the Japanese court, beginning with the rule that harmony should be valued and quarrels avoided. Its tenth article tells officials to restrain their anger when others disagree with them, reasoning that everyone has a heart and inclinations of their own, that none is wholly wise or wholly foolish, and that all are ordinary people. Some scholars think it was composed after Shotoku's death in his honour.
99.explanation: The constitution argued against angry words by appealing to shared human nature, asking officials to reason from their own fallibility to tolerance of others.
99.tie_back: The kural asks why anyone who knows the pleasure of kind words would deal out harsh ones, and Shotoku's tenth article makes the same appeal to self-knowledge against anger.
99._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a documented ancient text making a parallel argument from shared experience against anger, but it concerns resentment generally rather than harsh speech, and its authorship is debated.

100.event: On 13 July 1870 a telegram from Bad Ems reported to Otto von Bismarck a meeting between King William I of Prussia and the French ambassador, Vincent Benedetti, over the Spanish throne. Before releasing it to the press, Bismarck shortened it so that the king's courteous exchange read as a curt and final rebuff to France. The published version inflamed opinion in both countries, and France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870.
100.explanation: Bismarck deliberately turned a measured, civil message into a wounding one, and the result was a war.
100.tie_back: The kural likens harsh words chosen when pleasant ones are at hand to picking unripe fruit beside the ripe, and Bismarck had the courteous text in his hands and chose to publish the harsh one.
100._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of choosing harsh words over available mild ones, though Bismarck's aim was deliberate provocation rather than careless harshness.
